speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday during my absence the hon. member for Niagara Falls asked a question regarding the employment of civilian employees at Point Edward naval
Inquiries of the Ministry base near Sydney, Nova Scotia. As hon. members will know, this base has been used as the home base of the reserve fleet of the Royal Canadian Navy for a number of years. Owing to the present policy of having as many ships as possible in commission the number of vessels in reserve has been reduced. This year some ten Bangor type escort vessels were reconditioned for transfer to the Turkish navy. In order to accomplish this reconditioning in time 113 casual employees were taken on strength. It is expected that the last of these vessels will be handed over to the Turkish navy before the end of this month, as the Turkish crews are already in Sydney; therefore the work load in Sydney naval base will be reduced.
We appreciate that it is difficult for men to obtain other employment there, and a committee has been set up consisting of representatives of the Department of National Defence, the national employment service and the civil service commission to try to find alternative employment for these men. In addition there is a reconditioning program at the base starting at the end of this month, and a further examination is being made to see whether some more permanent operation may be established at that base by the reallocating of naval services from elsewhere. Everything possible is being done in order to find employment for the men who are now at the base. There have been no discharges made, and none will be made before the end of this month.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 14, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr-Mr. Sevigny in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the temporary extension of the seasonal benefit periods under the Unemployment Insurance Act for a six weeks period, from May 18, 1958, to June 28, 1958.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, under the rules of the house I have but a few moments left at my disposal. However, I propose at some later date, either during the resolution stage or when we are discussing

the bill, to make further observations in connection with this matter. But, taking advantage of the few moments that remain,
I should like to go back to the emphasis I placed yesterday upon the severity of the unemployment problem which now confronts Canada.
Possibly in this connection the committee would be interested in the April issue of the Canadian Statistical Review which has just come out today and which contains some very interesting statistical observations. It has to do with the percentage of people without jobs and seeking work in Canada. It shows that in January of 1958 the percentage figure was 201; in February of 1958, 202; and in March of 1958, 213. The index of 100 is based on 1956, which was the last full year of the last Liberal administration.
It is of the greatest interest that the figures published earlier, before revision, were as follows: January, 195; February, 196. The March figure shown above, namely 213, is a preliminary figure and it may well be higher than 213 when the revised figures are available later this month. Therefore, on the basis of this revision, the government is confronted with a very serious situation which will not in any way be obviated or minimized by the assurance of the Prime Minister that all is well and that the bottom has been reached. The evidence is that that is not so, and on this government rests the responsibility of meeting the mandate which was given to it by the people of Canada, based upon the assurances of the leader of the government himself that this problem would be resolved courageously.
We have no program put forward by this government consistent with those assurances. The day before yesterday the Prime Minister said that the measure now before us would resolve this problem of unemployment. I dealt with this situation yesterday but I repeat that this particular measure, welcome as it is to the extent that it goes, in no way resolves in any particular the problem of unemployment, the statement of the Prime Minister to the contrary notwithstanding.
In spite of what has been said by the Minister about the cost, the amendment will fall far short of meeting the need. It will do no more than allow supplementary benefit claimants who are on claim as of May 17 to continue after that date as long as their respective entitlements will permit. Many claimants will exhaust their benefit periods during the week of May 17. Some others may get an additional week, as the minister indicated yesterday, still others two weeks and so on. But it should be clearly understood that those claimants whose benefit

periods terminated at any time prior to May 17 will receive nothing even though they may continue to be unemployed.
That situation is a by-product of this measure, and I think the house and the country should know that the measure before the house does not go as far as the generalizations in the speech from the throne suggested on Monday last. I say to the minister that his figure of 200,000 persons who will benefit in part from this measure is undoubtedly a correct statement, if he says so, and what he says 1 accept readily; but I suggest to him that in order to give stuff to that statement we should know what "in part" means. What percentage of the 200,000 will receive the full amount during the period of six weeks? That may not be easy for my hon. friend to give, but in the absence of that reply the 200,000 figure must stand with obvious limitations.
At a later time I hope to indicate that I think the government has a responsibility to do more in this particular measure. That opportunity will come, but my closing words at this stage-I am sure the Minister of Labour will be the first to acknowledge what I am saying-is that this is not an unemployment measure but a relief measure. To the extent that it covers and gives assistance to those in need it will be welcomed on all sides of the house, but by no means, by no stretch of the imagination, can it be concluded that this measure goes as far as earlier indications seemed to suggest.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first may I say that this measure, limited as it may be, is certainly welcomed by both myself and my colleagues with whom I am proud to be associated. It seems that the history of this country has always been that every winter we have seasonal unemployment. That, I believe, was the basis on which the unemployment insurance fund was first established. In recent years, in fact three times since world war II, we have had quite severe recessions. Unfortunately the recession we are having at the present time has all the earmarks of that strictly forbidden word "depression". In fact I believe that only in one year during the 1930's, if even then, was the situation as serious or any more serious than it is today.
The hon. member for Essex East is a rather difficult man to follow because he has touched on almost every point that one might wish to bring up, but I think it will bear repetition that the measure before the house at the present time certainly does not solve the problem of unemployment.
In all probability it is not intended to do that. I should also like to stress the fact
Unemployment Insurance that it would be regrettable if wrong impressions should be created across our country by the way this measure was brought in and possibly the measure of publicity it received at that time. It could possibly create the misunderstandings that unfortunately were created when a similar measure was brought in during last session. I have met many people, and possibly other hon. members have also done so, who had the impression that they would qualify for benefits under the amendment made during the last session, but unfortunately when they applied for those benefits they found to their sorrow that they were not eligible.
Welcome as it is, this measure is nothing more or less than one extending payments for certain classes of unemployed. There is no provision for the unemployed without sufficient contributions. There is no provision for many of the unemployed whose benefits have already run out. I should like to know whether the government hopes to bring in before too long some measure to alleviate the condition of these classes I have mentioned. It is fine to help the ones this legislation will help, but what about the ones it does not touch? I am hopeful that further measures may be brought in at a later date in order to deal with those persons.
The Minister of Labour yesterday quoted a few figures. He said he hoped this legislation would benefit roughly 200,000 of our unemployed and that it would benefit them to the extent of $14 million. A matter of simple arithmetic tells us that the calculation works out at an average of $70 each for the 200,000 people. Spread over a six week period it works out at $11.66 per week. I am sure all hon. members will realize that with today's prices, $11.66 per week is not going to keep too many wolves from the door.
There is one other aspect of this measure about which I should like to have more information. It is not clear to me yet where this additional money is coming from. It has not been explained, at least to my understanding, whether this money is to be paid from the unemployment insurance fund or from the consolidated revenue fund. My understanding of the unemployment insurance fund is that it is based, dollar for dollar, on the contributions of the employer and the employee, with the federal government contributing 20 per cent of that total. I also believe that was the basis of the formula to meet the normal needs of seasonal unemployment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
That is right; take the case of Newfoundland.

Unemployment Insurance

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
I cannot help
wondering whether, if these additional or extended benefits are charged to the unemployment insurance fund, it will not tend to upset the apple cart. I know the minister mentioned yesterday that the fund was still in a fairly robust condition, but we also realize that it is possibly not as robust as it was a year ago. If this unemployment stiuation does not change, as we all hope it will, in a few months we could be in for serious difficulty.
I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that this should definitely be treated as an emergency amendment. This is not normal unemployment as we have known it in the past. An emergency measure should not be charged to a normal fund. It should be handled out of the consolidated revenue fund. It should not be handled by the relatively small numbers of insured people in this country. The emergency should be met by the people of Canada as a whole.
During the remarks he made yesterday my friend the hon. member for Essex East made reference to another matter which could be possibly of considerable benefit at this time, namely the abolition of the automobile tax. I might remind my hon. friend and other members of this house that we had in the last house a measure dealing with the reduction of the automobile tax and, if my memory does not fail me, I believe most of his colleagues voted against that measure.
I am glad to see the change of heart.
I should like to return now, Mr. Chairman, to this matter of the unemployed in this country who will not benefit from this measure. At the present time they are forced to fall back on the resources of their municipalities. I fail to see where the municipalities at the present time are any more able to meet this situation than is the federal government. The resources at their disposal certainly are not anything to be compared with the resources at the disposal of the federal government. I believe this matter is something that should be taken under consideration. The only hope, as far as the municipalities are concerned, is not that they are going to get any assistance but that at least their situation will not get worse with regard to those who will be able to benefit from this measure at least for another six weeks.
I hope the government will take these matters under consideration and make the necessary moves to alleviate the situation both of the unemployed and of the municipalities in which they reside.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
This legislation will be generally welcomed in my province where unemployment has reached unprecedented proportions and where, because of a curtailment in the woods operations and reduction of

employment on the United States bases, the prospects for employment are poorer than they have been at any time since confederation.
When the minister was speaking to his resolution he stressed the fact that the present formula will be used in relation to this extension. In that connection there are one or two questions which I should like to ask him, because I think they have an important bearing on the amount of benefit a person may receive from this legislation. As reported at page 85 of Hansard the minister himself quoted certain examples. Among them he stressed the point that this legislation would enable people to benefit who became entitled on the 17th day of May. If we follow the present formula, a person gets five weeks' benefit for six weeks' stamps, and he must have 15 stamps to quality. That means that the minimum entitlement that a person who is qualified can get is about 12 or 13 weeks. This extension will enable him to receive six or possibly seven weeks of his entitlement. The first question I want to ask the minister is what happens to the balance of his entitlement, the remaining six or seven weeks during which he cannot benefit under this extension. Will it be possible for him to carry over that entitlement into another benefit period?
The second question I would like to ask the minister is, what about those people whose regular benefits run out during those six or seven weeks, in other words whose regular benefits would run over into the extension period? Will they also carry on and take advantage of this extension right up to the end of June?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like
to thank the minister for having extended this benefit period, and I am very pleased to know that the benefits may apply to 200,000 people and give a benefit of $14 million.
In my area we have a serious unemployment problem, and the situation very much hinges on the problem of seasonal employment. During the past year the period during which our workers have been able to work in sawmills has been curtailed owing to lack of sales and in most cases they are no longer eligible, because of the short sawing season, for regular benefits. They have therefore depended for some time on seasonal benefits. I was very perturbed to find that after the last extension of seasonal benefits, when the period was advanced by one month and an additional month was added to the end of the period, these people were no longer eligible to draw seasonal benefits for the length of the benefit period.

I agree that if 200,000 people are eligible then we have done something, but I was certainly under the impression, as I think were many of my constituents as well as many of those people in other areas who were accustomed to drawing seasonal benefits, that if we extend the seasonal benefits we will be giving to those people who are seasonally unemployed the advantage of these benefits. There has been a great deal said right across the country with respect to a standing seasonal benefit taking care of the unemployed on this basis.
I think we should possibly consider the matter of again providing supplementary benefits and, if necessary, changing the basis of contribution so we can cover, on a supplementary basis, these people who are seasonally unemployed for the full length of time during which they are entitled to benefits.
The minister has said this is an emergency measure, and I feel that some consideration could be given to the fact that we could take additional money-the $14 million or probably a considerably larger sum-out of the consolidated revenue and put it into a supplementary benefit for the seasonally unemployed. If we did this we would not be hurting the unemployment insurance fund for years to come. I say this because, although the minister has said this is a temporary measure, I am quite sure if a similar situation arises next year there will be a great deal of pressure and considerable weight in the argument that the arrangement should be carried forward once again.
I think some consideration should also be given to changing the arrangements now in effect on the basis of the contributions. I am of course aware that this matter could better be discussed at various stages of the bill, but I do think some consideration should be given to industries such as the lumber and the automobile industries where lay-offs have taken place seasonally over the years and people have become more and more dependent upon what we consider to be seasonal benefits. Now, because of other curtailments, their periods of employment have decreased and their need for benefits has correspondingly increased.
If a person went on seasonal benefits-and many in the lumber industry in my area did go on seasonal benefits in the first week of December-then they are no longer eligible and will no longer be eligible under this amendment. In fact they have not been eligible for seasonal benefits since some time in early March. I think the impression has certainly been given to many people across Canada that the changes which were going 57071-3-7
Unemployment Insurance to be made would be much more generous than they have been, and would cover those who are no longer qualified for seasonal benefits in the regular way. If we now put into effect a supplementary benefit period, that would allow those people who for several weeks or months have been excluded from seasonal benefits to draw some assistance.
There is, of course, a method which could be used to assure them seasonal benefits at the present time. That method is provided for under the public assistance legislation, which of course goes into the matter of municipal assistance. I am aware that many, or at least some, of the unemployment offices have forms under that particular legislation, and these offices help the claimants who are no longer able to qualify for seasonal benefits to fill out these forms and they send them down to the town hall, after which the federal, provincial and municipal governments review the situation from the point of view of public welfare.
I am one of those who have paid into the unemployment insurance fund from the date it commenced, and I am sure that many of us who have never had and will never have an opportunity to draw benefits are benevolent enough to wish to see some change made so these people-and particularly the municipalities, who are ill-equipped to handle even minor expenditures on such a welfare basis- may be helped by taking some of the money from the general revenues and having it given to the commission to enable them to carry on with supplementary benefits for this period as requested by the minister. That could be carried out on a supplementary basis, in addition to the seasonal benefits, for those who have now exhausted their seasonal benefits.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as far as this measure goes it will, of course, receive the unanimous support of all hon. members. However, I want to be quite blunt and say I am very disappointed in what the Minister of Labour apparently believes is the necessary emergency measure at this time as an answer to unemployment in Canada when the seasonal benefits, as they are called, are running out.
When I think back to only a few weeks ago and remember how the hearts of the Conservative candidates bled for the unemployed of Canada; when I remember their platitudinous statements about what they would do for the unemployed immediately the House of Commons was called, should they be elected to power; and when I read the terms of this emergency measure as far as financial aid is concerned, I am unable to reconcile

Unemployment Insurance those bleeding hearts before the election with the action taken by the Conservative government after the election.
I think we all fully understand that unemployment is the measure or the scale of our economic trouble. There can be no question but that Canada faces a serious unemployment situation and, in consequence, major difficulties both for the country generally and for the unemployed in particular. Our unemployment situation can be broken down into two categories. I believe that a little less than 40 per cent of our working force are not covered by any unemployment insurance provisions whatsoever, and I cannot help but wonder just what thought, if any, the government has given to how that part of this 40 per cent who are unemployed are getting by today.
However, the resolution before us does not deal with this 40 per cent of our labour force which is not covered by unemployment insurance. It deals, in part, with the just over 60 per cent who do come within the provisions of the act, of which group many hundreds of thousands are today unemployed. These people have run out of both regular benefits and seasonal benefits, or are about to do so.
In an effort to take care of the situation to some extent the Minister of Labour introduced this motion, and we congratulate him on having done so. But while congratulating him on the distance he has come we should like very much to know why he has not considered the emergency in all its aspects, and taken the opportunity afforded by this resolution and the proposed bill to take action to guarantee at least a semblance of a standard of living so as to afford the basic requirements of life to all who come within the provisions of the act. Even with the provisions which have now been introduced many will not be able to carry on unless they can get work.
I find it difficult to understand the thinking of the government and the minister with regard to this matter. First of all we are told that this is a temporary extension of the seasonal benefit period. It will close on June 28 of this year. The minister obviously must realize that there will be many who will not have employment by June 28, nor will they be in receipt of benefits. But the fact that he uses the expression "temporary" can mean only one thing; that he is either fooling himself or that he is trying to fool this house and the public in general, because if he has the fantastic idea that there will be a return to economic and employment normalcy by June 28 he has another guess coming.
I wish he were correct. I wish it were not necessary to have an extension of the benefit

period. But if we are going to be honest with ourselves-and I think as newly elected members we should be honest-we must recognize that there is nothing temporary about the unemployment situation in Canada.
It appears, therefore, that under the principles of this resolution the Minister of Labour should have had the decency and the courage to face the facts and recognize that it is not only necessary to bring in a change in the Unemployment Insurance Act at this time to extend benefits until June 28, but that the proper thing to do in a civilized country under a responsible government would be to bring in the necessary changes to take care of the unemployed until such time as they can find employment. Must we be faced just prior to June 28 with yet another amendment to the act? I am afraid this will be the case unless the Minister of Labour decides to allow the unemployed to do without.
I wish to register strong objection to the policy of the government. I want to urge the government to face the economic and unemployment situation of this country in a realistic way, and give the people an assurance that satisfactory solutions will be found prior to June 28. I should also like to add to what has already been said by some previous speakers, namely that sympathetic though the administrators in the various provinces may be, they are governed by regulations made in Ottawa, and because of the way in which these are worded they will not be able to give assistance, even under these provisions, to countless thousands of needy unemployed in our country.
In the same way I have questioned the use of the word "temporary". I also question the use of the word "seasonal". The provisions of an act of this House of Commons or of an amendment thereto should be designed to take care of the unemployed no matter how long they are out of work. I am telling hon. members that a man can be just as hungry on June 29 as he can on June 28; he can be just as hungry in the fall as he can be in the winter, if he is out of a job.
I feel that not only in the last parliament but also in this parliament the government is making it completely obvious that it does not understand economics or the needs of the people of this country. Members of the government do not understand the broad principles which should apply to the care of our people if they are incapacitated, hungry or unemployed at any time of the year, and the sooner recognition of these needs comes about-and I am sorry such recognition is not evident in this measure- the better it will be both for the government and for the people.

That is the general principle. There is also a particular principle which may not apply in some of the provinces of Canada but which very definitely applies in British Columbia, one of whose constituencies I have the honour to represent. Seasonal unemployment is not based on dates that may be set by the Conservative government. Seasonal unemployment is based on the occupation in which you are engaged, and there are various seasons for each of the various occupations.
Let us take the fishing industry and lumbering operations as an example. Depending on the weather you can be seasonally unemployed in the winter but you can also be seasonally unemployed in the summer. Under the concept of the past and apparently under the presently existing concept seasonal unemployment is taken not on the basis of the occupation but on the basis of whatever date the government decides to set as the period when the individual can be unemployed and draw extra seasonal benefits.
If I correctly interpreted the speech from the throne I understand this is not the last time the Unemployment Insurance Act may be opened during this the first session of the twenty-fourth parliament of Canada. I can only say that we in this group welcome the advance that is being made, but we feel very sad at what is either the lack of knowledge of the present government or its lack of initiative, in that in the introduction of the emergency measure it did not spread the benefits to cover all emergencies in the labour field as far as unemployment insurance is concerned.
I recognize the sincerity of the Minister of Labour; I do not question that one bit. His sincerity leads me to believe that he will as speedily as possible introduce a complete overhaul of the act, bringing in major amendments; and when he does so I trust he will bring in an increase. I am sorry that none is provided for at this time. I feel confident that the ready acceptance that will be given the present change by all parties in this house will lead the minister to introduce the kind of changes to which I have referred.
I was in Winnipeg when the Prime Minister addressed the second national convention of the Canadian Congress of Labour. I sat in the auditorium as he spoke and I heard him waxing as only he can wax-and I mean "waxing" in more than one way- eloquently and telling the people of Canada to spend, spend, spend. I can still picture him as he stood there telling the people to spend. There are a few hundred thousand people in our country who do not have money to spend, and there are also a few hundred thousand 57071-3-7i
Unemployment Insurance who are dependent on unemployment insurance. They would like to spend, but the maximum they can get is $32 a week.
Mr. Chairman, I would like you to attempt to buy a house or rent an apartment in the city of Vancouver, for instance, and learn what the monthly payments would be. In many cases you would be required to pay anywhere from $85 to $140 a month. If you are unemployed and eligible for unemployment insurance you can receive a maximum of $32 a week. Thousands of families in my city find this amount barely adequate to pay their rent, their mortgage and bank payments and their taxes. There is little enough left over for food and clothing. And the Prime Minister asks them to spend.
It is easy enough for us in this house to get by, earning as we do between $10,000 and $37,000 a year, but the working class man who is buying a home and who unfortunately through no fault of his own is unemployed finds it difficult to provide for his family on unemployment insurance. I think it is the epitome of outright, damnable hypocrisy to go out, as the first minister of Canada did, and tell the people to spend, spend, spend and in that way work our way out of our present problems.
The government is now going to do some spending, which is fine and dandy; but it should give the many people on unemployment insurance a little more money to spend which would help them to restore the economic balance and give them something more than the amount of money required to meet their basic rent and mortgage payments.
I suppose it is useless to ask that an increase in unemployment insurance payments be granted today, but I hope this will be considered by the minister and speedily acted upon. I feel quite strongly about this. I feel I understand the problems of those who are unemployed, because I see them almost every day in my home constituency. I also met those who were not eligible for unemployment insurance because of technicalities in the regulations governing the administration of the act.
I welcome the present measure and will most certainly support it. I thank the minister for having gone as far as he did, and I hope he will take the opportunity in the not too distant future to correct his present mistake in not bringing in major amendments to the act and an increase in the benefits payable thereunder.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity of congratulating the Prime Minister on what I consider is his great personal achievement in securing his

Unemployment Insurance election as such. I am sure that great numbers of Canadians were very much influenced,
I trust temporarily, by his Lincolnesque vocabulary, his persuasive though somewhat ecclesiastical manner and his Shakespearean sense of the value of dramatics, phonetics and cosmetics. I am sure we all agree that without any doubt the Prime Minister provides a brilliant political facade to the economic deficiencies of modern capitalistic society.
That is the way we in this group look at it, Mr. Chairman. However, I am somewhat inclined to think that the Prime Minister's eminence is somewhat overemphasized by the flatness of some of the landscape around him. Nevertheless, in our opinion, regardless of his wishes and best intentions-and I give him all credit for good wishes and good intentions-he cannot under this system avoid being to some extent a political flockmaster for the economic barons of St. James and Bay streets. I hasten to say, however, that we all wish him well in what he does to offer us palliatives to partially remedy the evils of our present day capitalist society.
We in this group look upon this present measure as a palliative which will provide minor relief to a minority of the unemployed in Canada at this time. I am not going to speak at length on this subject, because other speakers in our group have advanced our point of view. However, before going on to my other few remarks, I cannot resist mentioning at this stage an editorial which appeared in the Trail Daily Times of March 8, 1958, a Conservative newspaper owned by the family of the Minister of Public Works, in which unemployment and the unemployed are dealt with.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR EXTENSION OF SEASONAL BENEFITS
speechtext:
I should explain in fairness that it is owned by a nephew of the hon. gentleman, if I am correct in my understanding, but in any event having some family association. In this editorial there is some criticism of the unemployed and reference is made to about one-third of the unemployed in Canada lacking initiative. The editorial says in part:
Unhappily, theirs is what appears to be a growing attitude among people today-the attitude that Canada owes its sons a living, and its older sons a pension.
Surely Canada, with all her natural resources, owes a living to anyone who is willing to work; certainly she owes the older citizens a pension. However, after berating the unemployed and then berating the party to which I belong and berating the present member for Kootenay West, the

writer puts in this article facsimiles of advertisements of job opportunities in Canada. Then he goes on to say that if people will only buy there will be lots of employment.
The job opportunities which he advertises in this editorial created a great deal of interest in my district. These are the advertisements for salesmen for garter belts, girdles, brassieres, real estate, Watkins products, unique promotion plan, door to door salesmen of other products. This is published in this paper, indicating the thousands of job opportunities that are available for the unemployed in Canada who will only show initiative. You know, Mr. Chairman, it reminds me of the Tory attitude years ago. I can see that the Minister of National Defence is not agreeing with me. I am sure many members of the Conservative party would not agree with this.
I remember reading the records of the House of Lords on one occasion. The House of Lords was dealing with an education act to provide free education for a larger number of people in Great Britain. This noble lord rose in the House of Lords. He was a very well known Tory with a record of great service to the empire and commonwealth. He said, "After 50 years of service to the empire and commonwealth and 50 years of interest in public education, and after witnessing the expenditure of a vast amount of money on public education, I and one of my associates have come to the conclusion that all we have succeeded in doing is lowering the level of the vulgar writing on the toilet walls about 12 inches."
That is about the attitude of some people toward the unemployment question. I give credit to the sincerity of those who bring this measure forward but we in this group believe these remedies are quite insufficient. They are temporary; they will improve things in some instances, but we simply are not approaching this question in a realistic manner.
The government suggests a national development and public works program. We have supported that because we need public development and public works; we need to put as many people to work as possible. That presents a limited scope from the point of view of sound economics and from the point of view of employing the largest number of people at this time. We in this group say that what causes our unemployment is simply surplus production which is not being sold at home or abroad. There is the whole basis of the reason for our unemployment at the present time. Here we have surplus wheat, surplus lumber, surplus metal, surplus fish. In our opinion the only sound remedy is a planned economic system

that provides for a sound expansion of our overseas trade. I am not suggesting this can be done overnight, or that it is a simple matter. On the other side of the world in Asia we have almost unnumbered millions suffering from the deficiencies of industrial production, food production and things of that sort.
I might say that while we support every effort to expand our markets in Britain and in Europe, this is a very well harrowed and ancient field which offers limited opportunities for the expansion of our markets for industrial and agricultural products. We wish the government well in what they can do in that direction, but it presents a very limited field. We say the markets in Asia present a great opportunity for us to do something within the reasonable future to remedy our unemployment situation and accept our responsibilities to some extent for international welfare and the welfare of other people.
We recognize the difficulties in this respect. It is not as easy to deal with these people as it is to deal with people who have sound currencies. We have not made an attempt in this direction. We know certain things can be sold for sound currencies, dollars, but they are in limited amounts. We say, as I have said before, we should first of all recognize these countries because they have certain sovereign pride and things of that sort, and you cannot deal effectively with people until you recognize them. It is not sufficient to send trade ambassadors up the back stairs and not recognize them officially if they get into trouble. We should recognize China so we could have an ambassador there, with consuls and commissioners.
. ^ read a statement about five weeks ago m which Mr. Mclvor, the former chairman of the Canadian wheat board, said that if we could obtain the Chinese market our wheat surplus would disappear almost overnight. There are three or four possibilities there. We believe there should be a recognition of those countries. We should do everything possible to expand our markets in Asia to relieve our unemployment. We should accept local currencies and have those currencies reinvested in local development, something after the fashion of the Colombo plan, and so on.
People say we cannot afford that. Is it better to afford that than to have 500,000 or 600,000 unemployed and idle people in Canada. We have calculated that if those people were all employed, if our farmers were producing at full blast and all the working people employed in this country, they would be paying income tax. The present
Unemployment Insurance unemployment is causing a loss to the Canadian people of somewhere between $350 million and $500 million in income tax. Is it not better to keep our farmers producing and paying income tax, and to keep our workers producing and paying income tax, and to use the surplus income tax we receive from this source and add it to what we have to stimulate markets in Asia along the lines I have suggested?
We in this group believe there is no other solution for the planning of our marketing. We should accept our responsibilities to the people of Asia, the underprivileged and underdeveloped countries of the world. We should sell our surpluses to them on a long-term credit basis and accept their currencies and reinvest them for their industrial and agricultural development. At the same time we should accept our responsibilities to the farmers and to the unemployed of this country. We believe that is the sort of plan that is essential if we are to commence to solve this recurring disease of capitalism, namely unemployment, which faces us at the present time.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I do want to say that we support this measure and we support all the other measures. I am not for a moment questioning the hon. gentlemen's integrity or their intentions or their best wishes, but we do want to emphasize the fact that they fail to realize that we are living in a rapidly changing world where, if we do not accept new principles, probably of a mixed economy, and a new basis for a trading relationship with Asia, we shall continue to have unemployment and we shall continue to suffer the disabilities of our national development that are related to it. That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief remarks concerning this bill.
In the first place, I wish to congratulate the minister for having brought in this amendment, just as I did when he introduced one last November. This November amendment was such as to bring help to a large number of seasonal unemployed, as the amendment proposed by the minister at this time will certainly contribute much along the same lines. However it will not solve the problem of unemployment in my constituency nor anywhere else in the country as a whole.
What we are voting at this time is nothing more than direct relief, such as was experienced under the Bennett regime, with this difference that between 1930 and 1935 direct

Unemployment Insurance relief was afforded to all unemployed who needed it whereas under the terms of the proposed legislation relief will only be given to those who qualify for seasonal benefits under the unemployment insurance act regulations. Now in my constituency as in the rest of this country there are a certain number of people who will receive no benefit whatever from the proposed amendment.
The other day I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) announce that there would be implemented in this country a program of public works designed to relieve unemployment. I have noted that among those that were listed, very few could directly solve the problem of unemployment in my constituency.
I would like the house to know that in my constituency, as in a number of others in the province of Quebec, most of the unemployed are bush workers, farm workers and workers in certain types of industry. The unemployment problem is more serious in the province of Quebec than in other provinces of this country. There are more unemployed in Quebec, in proportion to the population, than in the other provinces of Canada, a fact which is mainly attributable to a slowdown in the pulp and paper industry. The measure brought down by the government, that is the program of public works announced by the Prime Minister, will not solve the problem of unemployment in my constituency.
My constituency is served by three unemployment insurance offices. The southern half is served by the Hull unemployment insurance office, the Lievre valley area by the Buckingham office and the northern part of the constituency, extending from Grace-field north of Maniwaki, by the local office at the latter point. It is only from the Maniwaki office that I can obtain exact figures with regard to the number of unemployed, since those who live in the southern part of my constituency and in the Lievre valley area are served by the Hull and Buckingham offices, which also look after the unemployed from other constituencies.
I would like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that last week there were still more than 2,000 unemployed receiving unemployment benefits from the Maniwaki office alone. In my constituency, there are over 3,000 persons receiving unemployment benefits at the present time and I should like to point out to the minister-
How many?

More than 2,000 jobless come under the Maniwaki office. I should like to point out to the minister that, according to the officers in the unemployment insurance office in Maniwaki, there is in the northern part of my constituency, that is to say from Gracefield northward, a labour or working force of 3,500 or 3,600 coming under the Maniwaki office and that at the present time more than 2,000 of them are jobless. This means that over 60 per cent of the working population of the northern part of the constituency is jobless and I am convinced that, by June 28 next, there will still be over a thousand workers without jobs unless the government undertakes some public works in my constituency.
So it is my duty to suggest to the government some public works which could be of assistance in solving the problem and in giving jobs to these unemployed.
If the federal government could come to an agreement with the government of the province of Quebec or with municipal councils, it would be very easy to undertake road construction work as well as sewerage and water service works in some municipalities. Moreover, the Gatineau park, which is a federal undertaking, is in my constituency. All the government would have to do would be to grant a few extra million dollars to the Federal District Commission. Then, the commission could undertake to complete the park, which is part of the national capital plan. In Aylmer, last year, the municipality donated a beach to the Federal District Commission on the condition that a park and a public beach be set up there. Well, if the Federal District Commission had the funds required, it could undertake such works immediately. Other works which would be of assistance to the unemployed could also be undertaken in my constituency. You must not think, Mr. Chairman, that the building of highways into the Yukon, of a railway leading to the Great Slave Lake, an important extension of our airports and their equipment, as well as an intensification of harbour works, will solve the problem of unemployment. On the contrary this will help but a small proportion of the unemployed, not only of my constituency but of all constituencies in the province of Quebec and other provinces.
If the government really intends to solve the unemployment problem, to give jobs to the jobless, I urge it to undertake such useful public works in the various constituencies of the province and of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a suggestion which could very well be the subject of an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. In my constituency as elsewhere, many people cannot get unemployment insurance benefits; I refer to farm hands. At the present time, these people do not qualify for benefits and it seems to me that the time has come to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to cover them since, at present, many farmers cannot hire any unemployed persons, as these people, knowing that no stamps will be affixed to their unemployment insurance booklet, do not wish to work on the farms.
This situation is also unfair to farmers' sons who, instead of going to work in industries, remain on the farm to help their father and are thus deprived of unemployment insurance benefits. It seems to me that the law should be amended so as to include farm employees.
These were the few observations I wished to make. I urge the government to be kind enough to take into consideration the few suggestions I have put forward. In order to bring a real solution to the unemployment problem in the rural parts of the country, the federal government must co-operate with the provincial governments toward the implementation of a public works program capable of relieving unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, I can assure you right now that my remarks on the resolution before us will be very short.
My remarks are prompted by what the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) had to say yesterday when he proposed the resolution now before us, and I quote from page 85 of Hansard of May the 14th:
I would like to note that in the five months beginning December 1, 1957, and I think this will answer a question asked in the house earlier, almost $230 million were paid out in unemployment insurance benefits but in spite of these heavy expenditures the unemployment insurance fund had at the end of March a remarkably healthy balance of more than $740 million. We feel that this fund is therefore in a sound position to yield this extra protection which we feel should be provided and thus continue to do the Job it was intended to do.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we know that on March 31, 1957, the unemployment insurance fund contained $884,800,000 and, according to the minister's statement yesterday, on March 31, 1958, i.e. hardly nine months later, this fund had decreased to $740 million. And judging by the present unemployment situation in this country and by the number of
Unemployment Insurance unemployed who are receiving, and will continue to receive benefits, we may assume that the unemployment insurance fund, which was so sound when the Liberal government relinquished control to the present administration on June 22 last, would, on April 30 of the current year, have been reduced to $675 million, and before May 31 will probably have gone down to less than $600 million.
And if we may judge by the number of unemployed who I said, will probably continue to receive benefits, the unemployment insurance fund will be reduced by 50% by March 31, 1959.
I therefore agree with the previous speaker in saying that this legislation for direct relief is no different from the one passed by the Bennett administration except that, at that time, direct relief was taken from the country's general fund, whereas to-day it is paid out of money put aside by this country's workers.
I would like to close my brief remarks by quoting words spoken last Tuesday in Montreal by commissioner R. J. Tallon, who was representing the workers at the Unemployment Insurance Commission. According to La Presse of May 14, 1958, page 17, Mr. Tallon said:
It is unfair that the workers and leaders of industry should be the only ones to assume the cost of assistance to needy citizens. This should be the responsibility of the nation as a whole.
Which means of this country's government. (Text):

There are one or two questions that I should like to put to the minister and one or two observations I should like to make about the proposed amendment. Like other hon. members on this side of the house or, perhaps I should say, in this quarter of the house, I reluctantly support this amendment which is for the purpose of extending the winter into June. I think we should remember that that is its purpose. These seasonal benefits were established for the purpose of meeting the seasonal unemployment problem that is inescapable so far owing to our climatic condition in this country. It seems to me that, for a government that is obliged to say that the winter season is being extended into June, it is rather hard to argue that the economic situation in the country at the present time is not a serious one.
If the hon. member for St. John's West, the minister without portfolio, were in the house or if the hon. member for St. John's East were in his place, I am quite sure they

Unemployment Insurance would echo my words that in the province which we represent in this house the unemployment situation is very serious indeed. I think the minister is well aware that from the nature of things the amount of seasonal unemployment in that province, and perhaps to some degree in all the Atlantic provinces, is rather greater than it is in many other parts of the country. As a consequence, the number of persons capable of receiving these seasonal benefits because they have enough stamps to entitle them to receive the benefits and who are still receiving them at this late date must be very small.
In order to give us who represent that part of the country a clear picture of what it is the minister is asking us to do, I feel that when he replies or at some stage before this measure is passed he should give us this information. Of course, I should like to see the information for every province but I should particularly like to see it for the province of Newfoundland. I should like to know how many persons received seasonal benefits this year since the 1st of December, 1957, how many have already exhausted their benefits and how many are still receiving them. It may well be, as the minister has said-
In Newfoundland or in all Canada?

I should like the information for both. In fact, I should very much like to see it for every province; I should like to have it broken down by provinces, but that may be asking a great deal of the minister. However, I certainly should like to see it for Newfoundland. From the very large amount of correspondence I myself have received-and I know other members from Newfoundland have had a similar experience -it is my impression that the number of persons whose benefits have expired and have been expiring and who are now having to go on the dole is increasing very rapidly and has been increasing very rapidly ever since early March. There are some of us who were nasty enough to have the suspicion that one of the reasons the government was so anxious to dissolve the last parliament and have the election at the early and unseasonable date at which it was held was precisely that they knew that these seasonal benefits would expire and that there would be a great deal more discontent in the country in April than there was in March.

If the hon. member would
permit me to do so, I should just like to inform him that there has been a drop in

registrations in our offices across Canada to the extent of 120,000 in the last month, a more rapid pace than they dropped off last year at the same time, even without seasonal benefits.

I rather anticipated the
minister would say that. Perhaps he would tell us how much of that drop in registrations consists of fishermen who, of course, would be going back to fish and who would only have been eligible for seasonal benefits in any event; and how many others are in rural parts and who, once their benefits had expired and there is no reasonable prospect to their getting jobs from the offices, do not consider it worth while to keep their names on the roll?

If the hon. member would put
this question on the order paper I shall be glad to get the information for him.

The minister who is not
a new member of this house and who is asking us to take a rather extraordinary measure-
A proper measure.

-in extending seasonal
benefits that in a previous regime were required only in the winter time into the summer I think should not be telling hon. gentlemen opposite, the small band of people in the opposition, that they can wait for the order paper to get information relating directly to the measure that he is piloting through the house.

The former government left
the people destitute after April 15.

sitting down, although my hon. friend who very rarely makes a contribution in this house would like me to do so. I want to protest against the attitude of the minister in the course of this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
for Bonavista-Twillingate realizes that if he takes his seat then the minister can answer his questions. If he does not do so, he is not obliged to answer them.

I thank the hon. member
for Laurier for coming to my defence. I must say that I myself would have taken

no exception to the minister's attitude although I am afraid that it is a rather curious commentary, and not the first one in this very short period we have been here so far, on the attitude of the overwhelming majority.
Oh, oh.

First of all, on the very
day that the Prime Minister, with his hand on his heart, talked about extending the rights of parliament, an effort was made to prevent the opposition from having its traditional right, its fair share in debate. I know you are going to tell me I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, and 1 recognize the fact that I am. But today we have the minister doing what I really cannot complain of because I am afraid I have done it occasionally myself; I refer to interrupting in the middle of sentences in an effort perhaps to disconcert a speaker. However, I am not at all disconcerted. But what I am disconcerted about, Mr. Chairman, is the difficulty that there appears to be in appreciating what will be the real effect of this measure. Though I profess to be no expert on the Unemployment Insurance Act, it is very hard for me to conceive that there could be many persons who would have enough stamps left in their books to get seasonal benefits who would not have had enough stamps in their books to get regular benefits.
There may be the odd case here and there of someone who has had employment through the winter and who has lost his job in April or late in March but who would not yet have exhausted his seasonal benefits. But, as I understand it, the purpose of these seasonal benefits is to give benefit to persons who have not enough stamps to get regular benefits. The government already extended the season by something like eight or nine weeks during the last parliamentary session so it is hard to conceive how it could be possible that in this country where, the government says, employment is increasing rapidly, there could still be 200,000 people who could benefit under the proposed extension of this act.
I therefore think we ought to know a little more than we do about what it is the government is going to ask us to do and what the real effect of it is going to be before the debate closes. Even if only a few people will benefit it is, of course, a very good thing to do in the circumstances, but I have a suspicion that the number of people who will benefit from this measure is very small.
I do know that, in the province of Newfoundland at the present time

and I know this from correspondence I have received from people in my constituency since the election

that there is an increasing number of 57071-3-8
Unemployment Insurance persons who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits and are having to go on relief. This group increases every week. Fortunately in Newfoundland we have a reasonably well organized system of outdoor relief-rather better than that which exists in some other provinces-but still it is a humiliation for many people to have to go on relief. It is a regrettable necessity and it seems rather a curious commentary on the speech-and I use the word in the singular because it was the same speech-made over and over again by the Prime Minister only a very short while ago.
Before we go further in this debate, I think I should perhaps refresh the memories of some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house with respect to what their leader did say during the election campaign and the kind of appeal that was made and the kind of promise that was given on this question to the people of Canada. I have a reproduction of an article from the Toronto Star on February 28 last. The heading of it is, "Let No one Suffer is Diefenbaker's Pledge to Jobless."
Who wrote it?

It was written by Bruce Macdonald, a very reputable member of the press gallery who accompanied the Prime Minister over a good part of his tour, I believe, and I am sure the Prime Minister would admit he was an accurate correspondent. -it could not be denied that it did exist in some parts of Canada, for which the Liberals were to blame,-

-unemployment in March, 1955, stood at 9.5 per cent of the working force,-

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, what are the conditions in the riding which you represent, but I do know that in the riding I represent there are at present hundreds of people on the dole.

They need a new government, perhaps. I know 'that in the riding I represent and the ridings represented by the hon. members for St. John's there are hundreds of people on the dole.
He is doing something about it, though.

I can only say that those who are on the dole are suffering; perhaps not suffering actual physical privation, though some of them certainly are, but suffering because they want to work and there is no work. The Prime Minister said no one would be allowed to suffer. Then he came into the house the other day and used these astonishing works: "First, we meet the problem of unemployment by again removing the difficulties inherent in the extension of payments." This is how the suffering is being relieved.
I know the minister is not going to get up and tell us that even a small proportion of those people who are now unemployed will be covered between now and June 28 by this measure. The minister is an honest man and' I know he would make no such dishonest claims. But I do think that before we are asked to pass this measure the minister should give us some further information.
Of course, he cannot guess about the number of those who are not yet unemployed and who may become unemployed, but surely the minister would not have recommended this measure to the house if he had not found out from his officials how many people there are in the country today, or at the latest date for which he can get the information, drawing the seasonal benefits and, on an average, how much more benefits they are entitled to draw, whether it would be one week more or two weeks more; in most cases it would not be more. This is the kind of information which the minister should give us in some considerable detail because otherwise a false impression is likely to be created.
I had a letter from one of my constituents this morning from which I gather that this impression is already widespread. I know that what this man said was wrong, but nevertheless it is the impression which has been given. He said the government extended the benefits from March to May 15, but that "they won't give me any more". Of course he was not entitled to any more,

because he did not have the necessary stamps but many people have the impression that because this measure is being extended for another six weeks every unemployed person in the country will be looked after for another six weeks.
To the extent that this provision is helpful we welcome it, but I am afraid it will have a very small effect indeed in any part of the country. In those parts of Canada where seasonal unemployment is, on the average, more severe than in others, the effect will be less. Obviously it will have the most effect where there is the most regular employment and the least effect where seasonal employment is experienced from one year to another more severely, because in those areas there will have been less opportunity for people to have accumulated stamps in the past and thus become entitled to receive benefit.
I do not intend to labour this point but I should like to remind the minister again of the particular information which I should like to have and which, I am sure, other members from Newfoundland would like to have in so far as that province is concerned, namely the number of persons who have at any time since December 1 received seasonal benefits, the number who are still receiving seasonal benefits and, if they can be given, the comparable figures for the whole country. Those figures would be interesting, and I think the minister should also tell us his estimate of the period of time during which those persons now receiving benefits are likely to continue receiving benefits under this measure and also give us some kind of guess as to how many persons not yet unemployed may become unemployed and likely to be covered by these provisions, because, as I say, he is not likely to have brought in this measure unless some estimate had been made.
Of course, if there are no such persons, if the optimistic view which the minister expressed when he interrupted me is the correct one, and if no one is going to lose his job, that information will not be relevant. In such a case, however, I think the minister should tell us why it has been necessary to extend this period until June 28, because it is almost inconceivable that there would be any considerable number of persons drawing benefit now who would still be entitled to benefit by June 28.

A number of questions were asked and I will endeavour to answer first the question asked by the hon. member for Essex East. April 30, 1958. The estimated amount of seasonal benefits paid from December 1, 1957 to April 30, 1958 was $71,026,817. This is the last date for which figures are available at the moment.

You are a real Tory.

Will the minister permit a question? Even with the 200,000 receiving seasonal benefits under the new measure will there not still be more unemployed not receiving any benefits at all than there were last year under the Liberal administration?

Because they had jobs then.

However, some or all of the contributions that provided this entitlement may count for either regular benefits later or seasonal benefits next year. Just to clarify what the minister said, if a person has six weeks of unused benefits before he became eligible on May 17 can he use that six weeks to qualify next year or must he qualify first before he can use those six weeks?
It may count for either.

It cannot be anything else and what I have said is really a statement of the obvious.
