(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the workers of my constituency, I congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for introducing a measure extending by six weeks the period during which unemployment insurance benefits can be paid.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that all labour unions in Canada are happy to see that the Minister of Labour is asking for a six weeks extension of these benefits.
The difference between this government and the administration led by my hon. friends from the opposition is that the Minister of Labour is more readily able to cope with

Unemployment Insurance an emergency or to recognize when an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act is in order.
Therefore, on behalf of the workers of my riding, I take this opportunity to congratulate and to thank the Minister of Labour.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I indicated when I spoke earlier that I had some other remarks to make which, under the rules of the house, I was precluded from making because of lack of time. One could make them on the first clause of the bill but this would be just as convenient a point at which to do so.
I understand the difficulty that attends the minister at this time in answering some of the questions, particularly those that seek to elicit precise information as to the actual numbers who will benefit. The minister ought to indicate to his officials the desire on this side of the house for this information which I think could be given perhaps a little more precisely and in greater detail than has been given thus far.
The minister says that the number of people who will benefit in part is in the neighbourhood of some 200,000 individuals, and he gives as the total cost of the particular amendment before the committee some $14 million by way of estimate. I suggest that if 200,000 people are going to benefit, and if any of that 200,000 are going to benefit for longer than a period of a week, it cannot possibly be done at a cost of $14 million.
Last night I was trying to make some calculations and in my own amateurish way I came to the conclusion that it could not possibly be done unless the benefits for at least 75 per cent of the individuals were to be paid for less than a week, certainly not more than a week. Perhaps before we reach the bill the minister would inquire of his officials whether or not it is possible to give more detail with regard to this particular aspect of the problem.
The reason we are interested in knowing this is not only because of the obvious one. We wonder whether or not the fact that six weeks is the period selected does not arise so much out of a desire to help a group of unemployed who need assistance as out of a statement by the Prime Minister. To me the period of six weeks is an unusual one to take. It happens to be the figure that was pulled out of the air by the Prime Minister during the election when he was speaking in the city of Winnipeg and I wondered about it at that time. Knowing the Prime Minister's desire to give the impression that all of his promises are being fulfilled, it would not surprise me-and I am not now charging the

minister with this-one bit if the figure of six weeks was a figure selected not by the commission itself or not recommended by the minister, but selected arbitrarily by the Queen's first minister so that he could at some later date say, "Here again I have carried out my promise". I do not know whether that is so but it is a form of speculation in which I think the minister will acknowledge we on this side of the house, particularly at this stage of the new parliament, are entitled to indulge.
I mentioned to the minister earlier that there would be great disappointment if the extension of these benefits did not include those whose benefits run out prior to May 17.
It cannot.

The minister has indicated that it will not include them. I can only say that will mean that a very considerable number of people in this country, potential beneficiaries, will receive this information with the greatest regret. It certainly does not jibe-as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate indicated-with the promises made by the Prime Minister during the election. I have in my hand an unrevised book which contains the statements and promises made by the Prime Minister, not in the election of 1957 but in the election of 1958. I find, not from the Toronto Star but from an equally responsible newspaper, the Brantford Expositor, that the Prime Minister is reported on February 17 as saying:
Like Mr. Pearson, the Prime Minister said he does not regard the unemployed as mere statistics. He knew how grim unemployment was from personal experience.
"The humblest of our people will not be forgotten," he promised. "The people who are unemployed will not be put in the false position of being put on relief".
I ask the minister, is this particular measure a fulfilment of that promise? No one is going to be given relief; no one is going to be given the dole. I will see to it that you get jobs. That was the statement of the Prime Minister. Then, the next day, February 18, in a telecast made to the nation, the Prime Minister said:
Unemployment reached a postwar record of 520,000 in mid-January.
By the way, that was an understatement.
As long as I am Prime Minister of Canads everything that can be done-everything without regard to limit-will be done to the end that no one will suffer.
I am sure that the Prime Minister meant that. No human being wants to do anything that will cause others to suffer. But I ask the Minister of Labour, in view of the fact that a very substantial number of recipients of benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, whose benefits will run out before

May 17, will not be included in this measure, can it be said that this proposal is consistent with the assurances or the promises given by the Prime Minister to the people of Canada during the course of the election? I think that no one can confidently argue that that is so.
Then, on February 27, as reported in the Patriot of Charlottetown, the Prime Minister said:
I make this promise. We acted. My pledge is to every man and woman in this nation who is unemployed-so long as I am Prime Minister no one will be allowed to suffer in this nation.
I say to him that in those provinces where there is no public assistance measure and in the municipalities where there are no relief measures, or in provinces that have no relief measures and where they will not profit from this measure there will be people who will suffer. I know of people in my own constituency who will not qualify under this amendment and who will suffer and who will, as a result, not receive the kind of assistance which this measure seeks to provide. I say that in that particular the Prime Minister's promise to the people of Canada is not being fulfilled by this resolution. Then he said in Chatham, near my own city of Windsor, on March 5, as reported in the Chatham News:
But I say to them, unemployment is less today than in 1953, 1954 and 1955 . . .
That was not, of course, an accurate statement.
I know the needs of the humble . . . and as long as I am in power no person is going to suffer because of the inaction of the government.
These are some of the statements and there are many others. I say to the minister as a member of the government-I am not directing these remarks to the minister because he did not make these statements but through him to the Prime Minister-that this measure and any program of the government now known to the house or the Canadian people do not fulfil the promises made to the Canadian people by the Prime Minister of this country.
I suggest furthermore that instead of 200,000 people benefiting for a period of over 8 days there will be less than 40,000. I suggest that my hon. friend ascertain during the dinner hour before the bill is reached whether or not that calculation is not a more correct one.
I want to deal with something that was said by the hon. member for Timiskaming and the hon. member for Timmins. I think what they said was constructive and it was important that it should be said. This particular assistance is being provided out of the unemployment insurance fund, a fund now roughly
Unemployment Insurance $742 million, I think, a fund contributed to basically by the employee and employer groups of our country with a lesser contribution by the taxpayers of Canada generally. All groups are rather proud of the actuarial position of the fund. They are proud of the fact that this is something to which individuals have contributed themselves, something with regard to which they deserve the right of beneficial treatment as a result of their own contributions and hard work.
What are we doing? We are taking out of the fund moneys for the benefit not only of those who have contributed but for many who have not contributed to the fund, and the argument made by the two hon. members to whom I have referred is that this is a responsibility that should be borne not by two groups of the population but by the taxpayers generally.

I wonder whether the hon. member would clarify his statement that the fund will be beneficial to those who have not contributed to it, that people will derive benefit from the fund who have not contributed.

I am glad my hon. friend has corrected me. He is quite right, but people will benefit from the fund who have not contributed in equal measure. That is what I meant to say and that is important.
Mr. Pallet!: Which is quite different.

It is not quite different as I am going to show if the hon. member will just be patient. What will happen is this. This is the third time we have resorted to this particularly extraordinary means of dealing with the fund apart from the main provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is conceivable that we could have an abnormal unemployment situation year after year and that together with other intrusions on the fund the result might be that it might get down to a couple of hundred million dollars, let us say.
At that point the Minister of Finance will have to give consideration to replenishing the fund and I am sure if that time arrives there will also be a disposition to increase the contributions of employers and employees. I say that if that kind of situation eventuated it might be unfair to these two main contributing groups.
The minister may say that it was the government of the Liberal party that introduced the principle of seasonal benefits. That is true but when we did so we provided for grants made out of the consolidated revenue fund. We replenished the fund. We amended the act in 1950 to provide for the payment of supplementary benefits during the period January 1 to March 31. There were four classes

Unemployment Insurance to be covered, as I indicated yesterday, and two of those groups were covered by direct contributions of one cent each that were imposed on them to take care of the moneys being provided by that particular amendment.
With regard to the two other classes, and I need not give the details of their character, the minister of finance was authorized to transfer from the consolidated revenue fund a corresponding amount so that in no way was there any impairment of the unemployment insurance fund. That was likewise done when in 1955 the then government of the day brought in further supplementary benefits, and when Newfoundland entered confederation the unemployment insurance commission administered an unemployment assistance scheme that was financed out of the consolidated fund. That was what was done by the previous administration with regard to this measure and as a result of the steps they took the integrity of the fund was maintained.
Last year the seasonal benefit period was extended so that it commenced on December 1 and ended today and, of course, is now being extended to June 28. In addition, my hon. friend proposes a change in the formula for calculating the duration of benefit. The formula was one week of benefit for two weekly contributions. The formula now is five weeks of benefit for every six weekly contributions. The 1957 amendment made no provision for additional revenue to the fund to meet the cost of the new formula and the extended period.
My hon. friend estimates today that the amount of money involved in his proposal will come to $14 million. I have suggested that it could conceivably come to $25 million or $35 million if a substantial number are going to benefit for over a seven or eight day period. Last year the amount of the expenditure was, I think, $31 million. Whatever it was, it was a considerable sum of money. In any event, that was taken out of the fund and the government has taken no steps to replenish it.
It is clear that at some date this or some other government, in the event of depletion of the fund to a substantial degree, will have to take steps, but what I am pointing out is that at that time there will be a disposition to impose upon the two main contributing groups a further obligation and if the situation is as I am now describing I do not think that would be fair to them.
We have on the statute books now a measure that was designed for this very situation. We have a public assistance act which was introduced by the previous administration. That legislation was introduced so as

to impose the burden upon all the people of Canada and not only upon a limited number because the responsibility for maintaining those who need this assistance is a responsibility that does not belong to the unemployment insurance fund per se. It is an obligation that belongs to all of us and the principle behind the public assistance act was to do that very thing.
I know that the Minister of Labour has a very good answer, an answer which I would give myself if I were sitting in his seat, namely, that under that act as amended last year by the previous administration by removing the threshold it is up to the province to set the amount of assistance. At the present time no province pays assistance by way of relief to the level provided for under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Therefore I agree with the minister that in order to give the maximum measure of assistance to those who need it he is quite justified at this time in the circumstances, faced with the emergency, in using the unemployment insurance fund, but I say that at some time he should take steps to replenish it, if not now.
Then I say further that, having in mind the opportunity now at his disposal, he should take steps in negotiation with the provinces to see that they accept their responsibility in connection with this matter. I am sure that, for instance, in Ontario the reason why the public assistance act is not being used-I fully agree with the minister; and I know this because I heard the premier of Ontario say it when we were discussing this very matter in another room in this building-is that the government of Ontario did not want to pay relief payments that were at the same level as the unemployment insurance benefits. I say that it should be the objective of the Minister of Labour and of this government, in negotiation now with governments that are so friendly to them, to see that they increase their payments under the public assistance act to a level that will warrant on future occasions for these particular purposes the use of public assistance rather than the unemployment insurance fund.
But in any event, now that the minister has no other alternative but to use this measure, I say to him that the government at the same time should have taken steps to replenish the unemployment insurance fund to the extent that it was intruded on last year and to the extent that this year it proposes to intrude on that fund. It may be that the contemplated amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act will go in part toward that objective; I do not know. The minister may at some time perhaps indicate to us, if he can, what particular amendments

he has in mind, if the story is true that he does have in mind further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. But if the minister does not accept the suggestion that the fund should now be replenished and if he does not want to follow the practice which was pursued by the previous administration in this particular, I hope that the minister will at least say to us, as was suggested to him by the former member for Coast-Capilano last year, that at least very careful consideration should be given by the government and particularly by the Minister of Labour to the position of the fund in the light of this very serious situation that now confronts us and in the light of the possible situation which could eventuate on another occasion.
I think that the points made by the hon. member for Timiskaming, the hon. member for Timmins and others, particularly with regard to the fund, deserve support. It is for this reason that I have spoken about that matter perhaps longer than I should have spoken. But I say to the minister now before I take my seat that our position is this. We welcome this measure to the extent that it goes. We feel that it is not fair to give the impression that it goes farther than the general statement in the speech from the throne indicates. But above all, we take this opportunity of reminding the government of their own assurances to the people of Canada, of the pledges they made in the course of the last federal election campaign as a result of which they were accorded the largest majority ever given a political party in this parliament. The government has a very heavy responsibility. The only way in which it can be adequately discharged or honourably met is by the government giving leadership and really doing something to provide work, as it said it would, for the almost 600,000 men and women in this country who are now at this period without work. That is a responsibility that rests on the shoulders of the government. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution sets out practically word for word the actual bill which will be brought before the house. It deals only with one section of the National Housing Act, namely section 22 which is the section that provides for advances out of the consolidated revenue fund for the payment of certain loans.
The purposes for which this money has been used in the past are as follows: in the first place, it was used for making direct loans in the smaller centres of Canada, direct loans by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corpo-ation. In addition, it was used for what is called the limited dividend plan, that is, in assistance to the financing of the undertakings of companies which build low rental dwellings for old people and for low income families. A third use to which the money provided under this section has been put was to finance the building of rental housing for workers in primary industries; in the mining industry for example, in forest industries and other primary industries.
Under the act as it was originally passed in 1954 there was a total sum provided under this section of $250 million. When we took office last summer there had been spent for these three purposes I have mentioned, namely direct loans in small centres, financing of limited dividend corporations and advances for housing in primary industries, approximately $100 million so that there remained available under this section of the act about $150 million. This was the position in the summer of 1957; $150 million available for housing under this section.

We had not been in office very long before we found that there was a rapid falling off in housing construction across Canada. Lending institutions were advancing money reluctantly because of the tight money policy then in effect and this tight money policy was hitting the building industry harder than any other industry in the country. It was fairly easy to get a loan for an expensive home but it was very hard to get one for a small home. At the same time there was a great demand for smaller homes by young people wishing to buy their first home and by older people with modest incomes. It therefore appeared to us at that time that there was a great need for homes of this kind. Also, we began to see this dark cloud of winter unemployment coming up over the horizon.
For these various reasons the government adopted what we have called a small homes loan policy. We decided to take this $150 million which was available under the existing legislation and use it for lending out for the construction of small homes. We put a limit on the size of the homes; 1050 square feet was the maximum for a three-bedroom home, for instance. We found that this was the only fair way to impose a limitation because if we put a limit by way of money value then in some of the centres of Canada it would have been impossible for anybody to qualify. We also limited to 25 the number of loans that any one builder could get in order to spread the work out across the country and among various builders.
We made an agreement with the lending institutions of Canada, including the banks that they would act as our agents in the placing of these loans for what we considered was a reasonable fee. This meant we could get action quickly. They were in the lending business and we considered that the fastest way to get small homes under construction was to put out these loans under this agency plan.
When we adopted the plan we were uncertain that it would be a success. After all, we were very green in government but of more importance we were not quite sure we had found the right solution. However, we had splendid advice from the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and also from the lending institutions. We try to discuss these things frankly with the people in the business whose main function is to provide funds for the construction of homes and that has been our approach throughout.
The results of this policy have been extremely gratifying to the government and I think to all hon. members of the house. By the time November had rolled around we

found that the $150 million was rapidly being depleted. I would remind hon. members it had to be used as well for direct loans in the smaller centres and for the limited dividend corporations. We did not try to expand the loans for housing projects in the primary industries and that was a very small part of the business in any event.
Last December the members of that parliament were good enough to put through a bill increasing to $400 million the total amount available under this section. That meant an addition of $150 million. At the time we asked for this increase we also changed the down payments, the idea being that this would mean people with lower incomes, a group that had not been able formerly to take advantage of the plan, would derive benefit under the scheme. In addition to reducing down payments we increased the proportion of a person's income that could be spent on housing when the application for loan was being considered. I believe it was increased from 23 per cent of a person's income to 27 per cent. The decision with regard to this proportion, of course, really rests with the lending institutions some of which I believe are still working on the 23 per cent basis. One other provision was that work had to be commenced within a certain number of days. This restriction was imposed in order to get work under way during the winter months.
The plan continued to go well throughout the winter. Loans continued to go out and starts were made on new houses and finally we reached the position early in March when we had to stop putting out loans for the construction of rental apartments. About 20 per cent of the money had been used for financing small apartments although the main purpose was the construction of small homes. About a month ago the balance remaining became so small we also had to stop the loans for small homes. The loans for limited dividend corporations as well as direct loans in the smaller centres also increased in that period.
When we suspended the plan we had many applications in the offices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Applications came in very rapidly in April. I sometimes wonder whether some applications made under this agency plan should not really have been made under the ordinary National Housing Act insured loan. Be that as it may, when we were running out of money we went to the lending institutions and the banks and stated the problem. We explained that many people wanted to build small homes and requested them to take on the applications in order that no hardship would result and there would be no delay in the construction of homes in Canada. The institutions have responded very
National Housing Act
well and over 75 per cent of the applications with which we were unable to deal last month have been taken up by the lending institutions.
Perhaps hon. members would be interested in the figures which will illustrate what has happened to the $400 million fund. I have figures here as of May 9. Under the agency loan plan-that is, our small homes loan plan-$256,485,766 had been put out. Every cent of that sum has been put out since last August. I sometimes think when the opposition grow very critical of the government for doing nothing to provide employment during the winter they tend to forget that not one cent of this $256 million-odd would have been spent if it had not been for this small homes loan plan.

That will bring the total amount under section 22 to $750 million. This money will have to be used for the direct loans in small centres which are of great importance. We do not intend to have those Canadians who live in small centres by-passed in our governmental housing policy. Then, it will also have to provide for financing limited dividend corporations. We have done, and we shall continue to do, everything possible to encourage those limited dividend corporations. This is the plan under which a service club or a church may form a corporation to build houses for senior citizens. We think that these undertakings are of great benefit to the nation, and we shall give them every possible assistance.
It will also have to provide for continuation of the small homes loan plan which the government initiated last summer. We have as our objective the helping of young Canadians to build houses, the idea being to do everything possible to help Canadians to own their own houses; also to provide employment. I doubt whether there is any way in which jobs can be furnished more quickly than in housing, not only jobs for the men who do the work but also for the men and the women who make the furniture and all the other articles that go into a house and in the development of land, and so on. This particular activity in our country involves a great many jobs.
We do not aim to become the main source for housing money. The view of the government is that the bulk of money for housebuilding should be provided by the private lenders. It is hoped this year that there will be 140,000 housing starts in Canada. That will be a record. I think the nearest was about 137,000. As of today it looks as though that objective will be reached, by the way, in spite of all the hard-times talk we sometimes hear from-well, I will not say whom. subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Green -Mr. Sevigny in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1954, to increase from four hundred million dollars to seven hundred and fifty million dollars the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, together with a number of hon. members on this side of the house I have been given the responsibility of placing before the committee the viewpoint of the opposition on this matter. I confess at once that I am not an expert on housing, but because of the circumstances in which I found myself I have had to do a lot of reading in the last two days on the most interesting subject of housing. I found, much to my amusement, that I did not have at my fingertips the expert advice which I once had when I sat on the other side of the house and I recalled the words of a former member of this chamber, now in

another place, who one day stated here that it was almost like moving from a private car to an upper berth. However, I do not complain about the circumstances. In fact, in a sense I am somewhat happy because I am relieved of many responsibilities.
I recall some of the suggestions that were made to us by hon. members opposite when we sat on the right of His Honour about technical and expert assistance and I hope they will not soon forget the recommendations which they made in that respect from time to time. Although I am not an expert on housing I am convinced of one thing and it is this. We on this side of the house would like to see every Canadian own a decent home and we are prepared to co-operate with the government with respect to this measure to the degree to which it will provide that kind of housing.
The former hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount last year paid a tribute to the Minister of Public Works for the manner in which he presented the resolution he introduced at that time. I recall what a clear and lucid picture the minister gave at that time and he did the same thing shortly before six o'clock this evening and while I will not be able to commend him for everything he said I do want to commend him for the thorough manner in which he presented the resolution to the committee. I would not be fair to myself and to those who sit with me here if I were not to say he indicated in that presentation that he has a full knowledge of the subject matter which he was submitting to the committee. I thank the minister for the suggestion of co-operation on the part of his officials. He made a similar offer last year of which advantage was taken and we on this side of the house had the benefit of assistance from Dr. Bates, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and some of his assistants and I can assure the minister that that information was of great help to us. Had it not been for the short time at our disposal I am sure we would have again availed ourselves of that similar help this year.
I should like to tell the minister that he should not be too touchy about what was said in another debate about unemployment because nothing of that sort has been said yet in this debate. I am not guaranteeing that it will not be said but I am sure no one on this side of the house will deny that this is a good measure in principle which will tend to relieve unemployment. What was said earlier-and I hope I am not out of order, Mr. Chairman, when I refer to it-

was not in complaint of this particular measure but in discussion of the unemployment situation as a whole.
In breaking down the amounts of money that have been spent on housing in the several categories I believe the minister said some $392 million had been used up out of a possible $400 million leaving roughly $8 million in the fund. In effect, to use round figures, some $400 million was spent by the government since it took office with reference to housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE
speechtext: No; $100 million of that had already been spent when we took office.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Yes. I understood from the minister that when the government took office about $150 million was left out of the $250 million originally passed by the former administration. The point I was trying to make is this. Notwithstanding that expenditure in the intervening time from the month of February until March unemployment had increased by some 70,000 in this country. In fact, the figures given by my friend the hon. member for Essex East indicate that in the month of March, the latest period for which we had figures, the unemployment figure had reached 600,000. Surely this measure is going to be of assistance, and there is no doubt in my mind about that, but the position we have taken is that this is not enough. There must be measures of an additional character.
Dealing more specifically with the resolution now before the committee: It seeks to increase from $400 million to $750 million the aggregate amount that may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund under subsection 1 of section 22 of the National Housing Act. We are being asked to advance these funds to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the purpose of making loans as broken down by the minister earlier under the four headings he mentioned including agency loans, direct loans to small centres, limited dividend corporation loans, housing projects and the like. This measure is also for the purpose of making loans under section 40 and subsection 40 (a) of the act which is the section under which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been making a large number of the loans which are popularly referred to as agency loans.
The minister earlier this week stated in reply to a question that substantially all of the funds already voted by parliament have been used up and only a small balance remains, namely $8 million. As I understand the position it is this: unless parliament places other moneys at the disposition of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation
National Housing Act
it will have to discontinue its lending operations. We of the official opposition do not think this would be desirable and accordingly we have every intention of supporting this resolution and of facilitating its adoption by this committee and also of facilitating the passing of the requisite bill.
However, our acceptance of the resolution does not mean we have nothing to say on the matter of housing in general because we know the funds to be placed at the disposal of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be used to make various types of loans and that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation itself is only one of several kinds of financial institutions that ordinarily invest their funds in mortgages. The increasing of the funds to be available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is, therefore, in our view the appropriate occasion to review the housing situation generally and that is what I would like to do now dealing with certain points as briefly and as factually as I can.
In that connection I believe I should sound a note of warning because it is quite clear from what was said by the Prime Minister and other prominent Conservatives during the election campaign that they believe their actions in providing substantial funds for housing have been of invaluable assistance to the economy generally. I shall not deny that the loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have had a beneficent effect on the building of new homes but the facts as to mortgage lending in Canada last year make me wonder whether the government's intervention in this field, hitherto occupied almost exclusively by private institutions, has not merely had the effect of encouraging these institutions to seek other forms of investment for their funds.
I have here the Canadian housing statistics for the fourth quarter of 1957, published by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They show a number of things which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. They show firstly that in 1957 the life insurance companies and the trust, loan and other lending institutions invested $239.3 million, which was not much less than the $254.9 million they invested in those mortgages in 1956. These figures can be found on table 17 on real estate lending. Secondly, I should like to say that in 1957 the chartered banks actually increased the amount of their loans under the National Housing Act. The amount of such loans approved in that year was some $15 million greater than in 1956. As a matter of fact, as shown on table 18, this amount was $173.5 million as against $158.2 million. Thirdly, the loans under the National Housing Act made in 1957 by the life insurance companies and

National Housing Act
the trust, loan and other lending institutions dropped very substantially. Whereas those lenders had invested $267.1 million under the National Housing Act in 1956, they invested only $104.6 million in 1957.
This, hon. members will agree, is a very big reduction and one cannot avoid asking oneself what is the reason for it. The answer seems to be suggested by the statistics which show that in 1957 Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loaned $235.2 million in contrast to $19.9 million in the previous year; in other words, the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has not only made up for the reduction in lending by the private institutions, but has lent more than $100 million besides.
I realize the difficulty in establishing positively that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation activities account for the reduction in private investment and therefore I shall not attempt to labour the point any further. However, it will be sufficient for me to state and to draw to the attention of the government the dangers of it coming to occupy a preponderant or overdominating position in this field.
There are advantages in encouraging institutional lenders who favour this type of investment, and not the least is the advantage which comes from the fact that these lenders are very sensitive to indications that in any particular locality or in any particular type of accommodation there is over-building.
The next point I wish to touch on is that the building of new houses affords good employment opportunities and for that reason I consider it important not only that the government should be able to make loans, if and when that is desirable, but also that it should not discourage the traditional lenders in the mortgage field.
Throughout the election campaign and since the government has emphasized the value of its lending activities as a means of providing employment. But having regard to the numbers who have been out of jobs I am very much surprised that at the very time the government was proclaiming the virtues of its lending program as a make-work project it was positively discouraging the building of rental accommodation.
Early this year builders were told-they were encouraged-to submit plans and specifications to those making the agency loans, and they were led to believe that their applications would be given favourable consideration. Many builders went to considerable trouble and expense to prepare plans and specifications and then without warning the lending institutions were advised that the agency arrangements for rental loans were terminated.
I hold in my hand the directive, or the advice, given by the executive director of the corporation in this regard. It is too long for me to read. Suffice it to say that this action was intended to conserve finances for home-ownership purposes. The minister touched on that earlier, but surely it is a rather highhanded way of proceeding, particularly when it seems desirable to encourage all forms of building as a means of increasing employment, and as the need of rental units is very acute in many places and in some cases greater than single family residences.
If the placing of these funds at the disposal of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation means more work and more employment in one field, it is difficult for me to understand why one should discriminate against rental housing in favour of single-family houses because one provides just as much employment as the other. In fact, I am told that the former provides more work than the latter.
This brings me to another point, namely that there is a real need to give attention now, having regard to present levels of employment, to the question of slum clearance and to the building of low-rental accommodation. I should like to remind the committee, if I may, that after the convention of the Liberal party which was held in Ottawa in January, several resolutions were adopted but one particularly having to do with housing. I do not want to labour the point, but I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the preamble of the resolution and to one or two of the items that had to do with housing.
Because of the importance of good housing to our way of life and to the health and happiness of Canadians, the Liberal party has as its goal the provision of a decent home for every Canadian.
Accordingly we on this side of the house stand for that measure and we stand also for the encouragement of the building of moderate and low-rental accommodation by increasing the maximum loan. We are in favour of introducing a municipal grants assistance act under which the federal government would assist municipalities in the installation of essential services. We would like to extend the participation of the federal government in slum clearance and urban redevelopment programs by increasing the federal government's share of the cost of acquiring and clearing blighted or substandard areas, and in special circumstances by lending to the municipalities their share of the cost of such projects. We would increase the federal government's share of the cost of constructing low-rental subsidized housing for low-income families.

National Housing Act
I hope, therefore, that the government will later this session introduce further amendments to the act, designed to make federal assistance greater and its co-operation along those lines more effective.
I come now to another point which I think should be of great interest to the committee and, of course, to the minister, namely the rate of interest to be charged on loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. During the election the Prime Minister repeatedly stated that as a result of government action since last June interest rates had fallen sharply. At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I should like to assure the minister that the group in this corner of the house is in wholehearted agreement with his main aim of obtaining this additional money for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I was very much interested in the minister's remarks this afternoon. I was also very much interested in the minister's remarks because it was an amazing half hour. It was almost like a chinook out west where for one hour you have a temperature of 30 degrees below zero and then for several minutes you experience a temperature of 30 degrees above zero. The minister seemed at times to be one of the finest advocates of socialism in this house that I have heard for a goodly number of years. Yet every once in a while he insisted that he was a genuine free enterpriser after all; he only regretted that free enterprise was not meeting the housing needs of the Canadian people and therefore he was by force of circumstances a very good socialist and was pleading with the house to be socialist with him.
The minister reviewed the act since 1954 and he listed the uses that had been made of the money that had been made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He mentioned the direct loans in smaller communities, the limited dividend plan for low rental houses and, as a third, he listed the fact that the money had been used for the building of low rental houses for workers in primary industry. I believe the minister forgot to mention a fourth use that was made

over a goodly number of years, namely a time when the money supplied by this parliament was used to supply a nortion of the regular loans that were made by the private lenders. I believe it was 25 per cent of all loans made under the act by private lenders at one time.

which was an appeal to private investors of Canada to make available enough housing money so that 3J million new homes could be built in this country in the next 23 years. With a rough bit of arithmetic it appears that he would mean by that 150,000 housing units per year. I am afraid that our experience over the last several years has shown that the mere appeal of government members or civil servants at annual meetings and the like for investment in housing is quite inadequate. Investment capital naturally flows where it earns the highest return and, as the minister very well knows since he was in the house with me during the last several years, when the earnings of Canadian enterprises began to rise, especially after the reduction in corporation taxes allowed by the former government, the interest of people who had investment capital at their command began to move away from the orthodox fields of investment and in the direction of industrial expansion because the return there was so much higher. In such cases as public and private utilities investment was at least as secure as it was in housing. At such times the former government became quite frantic and appealed in similar terms to the appeal made last night in Ontario and to the minister's appeal in the house this afternoon. They appealed to the managers of investment capital to make more provision for the housing needs of the people but their appeals fell on deaf ears and did not bring about the desired results. So the former government finally found a new source of capital for housing.
The chartered banks of Canada have never been primarily interested in the investment of capital in long-term industrial expansion and the government realized that these banks, because of our economic expansion, were a little flush with funds. The chartered banks were then put into the field of housing and that arrested the decline in housing for a time, but only for a time. It was not very long before the banks had invested what they considered to be an equitable and safe share of their assets in housing. The earnings of corporations continued to increase and less and less private money was made available for housing. These pious hopes for the social needs of Canada being met by mere appeals at annual meetings will not bring money into the housing field, and we must have that money.
It is for these reasons we have always advocated a national investment board whereby the government of the country would assume some responsibilty for the direction of the flow of investment capital and would see that there was a rational distribution of the

available investment capital at all times. I know this would involve amendments to several acts. The Bank Act would likely have to be amended; the act respecting loan companies would have to be amended and the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act would require an amendment, and other acts would have to be amended. There are, however, ways and means available to the government whereby it could exert the pressure necessary to be exerted on managers of investment capital to ensure that we will not have a reckless expansion of certain segments of our industrial enterprise-often to our own regret later on when we find we have not the markets to handle increased production-and to ensure that enough money will be available where it is most urgently needed in the public interest.

Might I ask my hon. friend a question? Getting back to the subject of the bill, I wonder if my hon. friend would indicate to this side of the house whether or not he is in favour of the bill before us because, so far, none of us have been able to determine that.

Experience has shown this to be the case as the minister knows full well. As a matter of fact, private enterprise suddenly lost all interest in investment in housing in Canada about a year ago and it took quite a bit of aggressive action on the part of the minister-and I would like to give him full marks for this-to make more money available. However, if he feels that the making available of $150 million or $350 million is going to prevent a slump in housing, all I am saying is that this is not necessarily the case. It all depends on where the other 75 per cent of the money is going to come from. If the earnings of the Canadian corporations are going to be allowed to rise again, as they

have done on other occasions, the minister six months hence may find himself suddenly left holding the bag with his 25 per cent and he will find that the other 75 per cent of the money on which he had relied to meet the needs of our people has vanished.
I hope we will have another chance to discuss the act but I do regret that the minister has not yet seen the need to supply insurance policies under the act, insurance for the buyer as well as the lending agency. It is becoming a very common practice in this country, wherever there is a new housing subdivision, that two or three days after the new home owner has moved in there is a knock at the door and an agent, very often the agent from the very life insurance agency which has handled the mortgage, calls and is able to convince the new home owner that he should buy a life insurance policy which will retire the mortgage in the case of his death.
I feel that is to be regretted because under the act the buyer has to pay a premium which insures the lending agent against default, against inability of the buyer to meet his monthly payments. However, there is nothing in the act to give adequate protection for the buyer's equity in his new home. I feel that even if a slight extra rate in this insurance premium is necessary, the government might be able to supply this added protection for the occupant of the new home.
I note again, as I did last year, my concern that much of the success of the minister's program has involved a reduction in the size of the home. Many people in Canada have commented to me about the dangers involved in building units of hundreds upon hundreds of new homes which are limited as to floor space in relation to the number of rooms provided in the houses, and there is a fear abroad that these homes may end in years to come as areas which we sometimes refer to as slum areas. This may be part of the price we have to pay for an aggressive home building program. I do not know. But I regret it if this is one of the sacrifices we have to make in order to obtain homes for our Canadian people.
I have not yet looked at the minister's estimates but I hope he is going to ask for more money for the research department of the C.M.H.C. We have made tremendous technical advances in almost every field of activity, yet when it comes to building a home we are using almost the same techniques as we used 40 or 50 years ago. I do not know where the bottleneck is, but I hope the day is not far removed when we shall see some technological advances applied to the building of Canadian homes, because it is the high cost of homes which is primarily responsible for many of our difficulties.

I was a little surprised by the lack of logic or commonsense shown in a portion of the remarks made by my old friend the hon. member for Laurier. He began by criticizing me very severely for having the government do all the lending. He said: You should let the private institutions do this lending; you are going too far; you are getting the government into this field too deeply. And then, after he had made a few other remarks and forgotten what he said in his opening, he told me: you had better drop the interest rate; you are charging too much; there has been a decline in general interest rates, so why do you not lower the interest rate on housing.
The hon. gentleman cannot have it both ways. If he wants us to get the lending institutions to put up more money for home building the finest way to fail in that objective would be to drop the interest rate, because the problem has been that where the lending institutions can get a higher rate of interest in some other investment the tendency was to put their money into that other investment and not into housing. I am sure that upon reflection the hon. member will appreciate that this is the situation. Were we to announce tonight that the interest rate on N.H.A. loans is to be lowered it would be

National Housing Act
just that much more difficult to get mortgage money from lending institutions. As a matter of fact the present rate is well within the statutory provision and I think it would be doing a great disservice to the country if I were to announce a drop such as the hon. member for Laurier has suggested.

I do not pretend to be able to prophesy what effect it will have on the money market, but I am sure it will have a good effect in providing homes for young Canadians. I did not deal with that subject because it does not come under this particular section of the National Housing Act. These redevelopment schemes are joint federal, provincial and municipal schemes. Money is provided quite apart from this particular section, so a discussion of that subject was not relevant in the debate before the committee this evening. The hon. member read me part of the platform which was passed by that ill-fated convention last January. The actual fact is that we are very much interested in redevelopment schemes and are doing our best for them. For example, there is a redevelopment scheme in Halifax and I signed the agreement for the dominion government last month. Then again, we are going ahead with the Jeanne Mance project in Montreal. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention tonight to speak at great length on the resolution that is now before the committee. As the minister has just said, we will have other occasions in the future to discuss the whole housing situation. In addition to that, when a similar measure was introduced last December I had occasion to make some remarks and suggestions on the subject. At that time I said that although more millions were placed at the disposal of prospective borrowers it does not mean that many more people with modest incomes will be in a better position to take advantage of the provisions of the act. Those words can be repeated with even more significance today.
Although I am in favour of this resolution I think it does not go far enough and consequently it does not reach the real purpose of the act which is to provide a decent home for every Canadian. For example, how can a prospective borrower secure a loan of $9,000, if his weekly salary is $65 which is the average salary in the province of Quebec? He will be advised by the banks or the lending institutions that they cannot grant his request because the monthly payments will be not less than $78 or $80 to amortize the capital and pay off interest and taxes; and this amount of $78 or $80 does not take into account the ordinary expenses for the maintenance of the house. It seems logical to assume, therefore, that a borrower who wants such a loan will have to earn a salary of at least $85 a week. Moreover, according to the latest information I could obtain the average income of people who bought houses under the act last year was $5,857.

It seems that the lending institutions have a certain reluctance, or are not interested enough, to make loans for the construction of houses in those areas. I am quite certain that many hon. members who come from small cities are aware of this fact and I can see no reason why those thousands of Canadians living outside of large metropolitan areas, who also pay taxes, should not benefit equally from the money that is supplied by our own government.
For instance, if one refers to the report published by the bureau of statistics, entitled, "New Residential Construction, March 1958," he will find that more than 80 per cent at least of the dwellings that were started or completed between January 1, 1958 and March 31, 1958 are located in metropolitan areas. In this pamphlet on page 9 there is table No. 3 having to do with construction of dwelling units in urban centres of 5,000 and more. If one looks at the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, he will find that under construction of dwelling units from January 1 to March 31 of this year out of 96 starts, 84 were in the city of Halifax. In Ontario the situation is exactly the same as far as proportions are concerned. Eighty or 85 per cent of the starts and completions took place in the metropolitan areas of Hamilton, London, Ottawa and, of course, particularly Toronto. We have one of the best examples when we come to the province of Manitoba. Out of 265 starts, 263 were in the city of Winnipeg and out of 612 completions, 545 were also in the city of Winnipeg.
I hope that the Minister of Public Works, who I know is taking a good deal of interest

National Housing Act
in this question, with the help of the experienced officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will find ways and means to improve the situation in this regard. May I assure the minister at this time that I am not doing this in any critical way, but I am trying, as he asked us to do, to put up some constructive suggestions.
There is also another reason why many cities and municipalities are unable to take advantage of the act, namely that very often they are unable to finance the installation or extension of essential services. I believe it is the responsibility of the senior governments to see to it that their growth and development are not retarded just on account of their inability to pay these costs. I am quite sure that most hon. members have in their constituencies, cities or towns which fall into that category. Surely, and particularly in this difficult period when there are hundreds of thousands of unemployed persons all across Canada, the federal government, in collaboration with the provinces, would be more than justified in giving financial assistance to the municipalities.
I think that now it the time to introduce some kind of legislation or to amend the National Housing Act to assist municipalities in the installation of trunk sewers, water mains and other essential services or, on the other hand, make available to the municipalities the benefits of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act, which was passed by the federal government in 1938. By that act the Minister of Finance, with the approval of the governor in council and, of course, subject to the provisions of the act, could make a long-term loan to a municipality to enable such a municipality to pay the whole or any part of the cost of construction or extension of projects that would be self-liquidating.
The rate of interest at that time was 2 per cent. I do not want to say that it should be 2 per cent today, but I think the government should help in supplying more money to the municipalities to undertake such projects at a reasonable rate of interest.
I have with me a copy of the report on the operations of this act for the year ended December 31, 1957. Of course, lending operations under this act ceased some years ago, but it is interesting to note the variety of projects that were undertaken with its assistance. Applications were made for installation and extension of water and sewer mains, filtration plants and reservoirs, pumping stations, street paving and many other kinds of projects which are related and are needed when a city or a municipality wishes to develop a certain area for new housing construction.
[Mr. Bourget.l
In the province of Quebec applications were approved for nearly $2 million at that time. This shows clearly that that kind of legislation was greatly beneficial to the development and growth of our municipalities. I hope the minister will give serious thought to this suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, another point which, to my mind, is of the very highest importance with regard to this important matter of housing is that of the interest rate paid by the borrower.
In December last, when I took part in a debate on a similar measure, as I recalled at the beginning of my remarks, I had asked the government to lower this rate, at least with regard to those who earn less than $5,000 a year. Today I wish to renew this request, in even stronger terms. I would like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) to see to it that the interest rate is lowered in appreciable proportions, especially since, at this time, the cost of money is on the decrease. We should also-I do not want to labour this point since I dealt with it last December-extend the amortization period in order to help those with modest means to meet their monthly payments. Otherwise, if the interest rate is not decreased, if the amortization period is not extended, this will prevent most wage earners from taking advantage of this legislation.
All those who are interested in this matter keep pleading the case of people who, because they earn little, find it hard to secure loans.
No later than this morning I read in Le Devoir, on the editorial page, the following remarks:
In 1957 the demand for long term credit was quite high thereby bringing about an increase in the interest rate, which fell however towards the end of the year. This caused a decrease in mortgage funds provided by lending institutions. To correct this, the interest rate authorized with regard to loans under the National Housing Act was raised to 6 per cent.
On the other hand, the down payment was reduced to such an extent that the act now allows the loan of 90 per cent of $12,000. Such a mortgaged debt at 6 per cent, even spread over 25 years, is excessive for three out of four wage earners. More and more, the average income of borrowers under the N.H.A. exceeds the average income for the whole of Canada. In 1950, the average income of borrowers was $3,638. It reached $5,312 in 1956 and $5,857 last year.
It is therefore obvious that, if the situation is not remedied and if the interest rate is not reduced, it will become increasingly difficult for those who really need it to qualify under the act.
In the province of Quebec, as I said to the hon. minister in December last, his task would be easier if, with the help of his colleagues from Quebec who are now more numerous

in this house, he could convince the premier of that province to grant an interest rebate also to the people of that province who wish to borrow under the federal guarantee. Such efforts will be easier now that his friends in Quebec no longer consider the federal government as a foreign government.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all hon. members realize the great importance of the housing problem, having regard especially to its effects from the social point of view. That is why I wanted to make these few remarks today, hoping that the government will propose the improvements which are absolutely necessary.
